All three are `hard_case` kinds emitted by the substrate under [CC 3.4.4](part_3_the_namespace.md#3.4.4).

**The accord's holders are no family record (normative).** The accord is the lineage of a genesis bundle ([CC 3.2](part_3_the_namespace.md#3.2) T5, [CC 2.6.1.11](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.6.1.11)). Its holders are the bundle's `holders`, and a strict majority of the holders of the bundle in force decides ([CC 4.2.6](part_4_composition_governance.md#4.2.6)). The bundle's `family_key_id` is the lineage's name. It is no group id, and no group is founded under it.

**Worked example — household with self-devices and family-devices**:

```
User Alice has:
  identity_key = alice_root_key

Alice's self (identity_occurrence members):
  - alice_phone_key      (device_class: phone)  -+
  - alice_laptop_key     (device_class: laptop)  | Each is an identity_occurrence
  - alice_work_laptop    (device_class: laptop)  | of alice_root_key per CC 3.3.6;
  - alice_homeserver_key (device_class: server) -+ content Alice keeps on her phone
                                                   is cohort_scope: self and reaches
                                                   her other devices via the at-rest
                                                   encryption flow.

Alice's agent: alice_agent_key, its own identity, owned by
  Alice by an owner-binding (never an occurrence of hers); within
  her self for delivery unless she excludes it (CC 4.4.3.19).

Alice's household (a family subject_kind instance):
  family_key_id: <the id derived from its founding>
  family_name: "Acme Household"
  members: [
    {key_id: alice_root_key, role: founder},  -+
    {key_id: bob_root_key, role: founder},     | Member entries are IDENTITY keys
    {key_id: living_room_tv, role: member},    | (NOT occurrence keys). Bob has his
    {key_id: kitchen_tablet, role: member},    | own self-collective; the TV and
    {key_id: hall_thermostat, role: member}   -+ kitchen tablet have their own
                                                 identity_keys (they don't belong
                                                 to any one person via identity_occurrence;
                                                 they're shared household nodes that the
                                                 family has admitted as members in their
                                                 own right).
  ]
  consensus_protocol: "founder_only" // either founder admits new members
  consensus_protocol_entrenched: false // founders can amend the protocol

When Alice's phone sends a family-scoped photo (e.g., dinner photo) at
cohort_scope: family + family_id: <that derived id>:
  - Substrate wraps the DEK to each member's live occurrence encryption keys, one key_grant:content:v1 row per recipient (CC 3.3.2); a member whose occurrence carries no ML-KEM-768 key is fail-secure excluded
  - Photo bytes reach Bob's devices, the TV, the kitchen tablet,
    the hall thermostat — every admitted family node
  - No holding claim leaves the family (CC 5.2); non-family peers
    cannot even discover the content exists
  - Alice's own laptop also receives the photo via the at-rest encryption
    flow at cohort_scope: self → identity_occurrence

When Bob's mom Carol visits and Bob wants to admit Carol to view
family photos for a week:
  - Bob, an active founder, emits a membership:proposal to carol_root
    (role: member, expires_at set)
  - Carol answers with her own membership:acceptance naming that
    proposal, signed on her phone — no one is seated without the
    joiner's acceptance, and a node gives none (CC 3.1.3.2)
  - a membership:widening seating {key_id: carol_root, role: member,
    valid_until: +7d} is cosigned under consensus_protocol "founder_only":
    Bob's signature as an active founder satisfies the protocol
  - each photo owner's substrate, as sealer, emits retroactive key_grants
    for its cohort_scope: family content to Carol's live occurrences
  - At valid_until the seat lapses; an earlier exit is a membership:removal
    under the protocol or Carol's own resignation. Either way Carol retains
    existing key_grants per CC 4.4.3.22; substrate stops wrapping new family
    content to her key
```

The example demonstrates the clean orthogonality: **`identity_occurrence` is for participants that ARE me** (across my devices; an agent binds its own identity, [CC 3.3.6](#3.3.6)). **`family` is for trusted nodes that compose with me** (other people's identities, shared household devices, multi-party collectives). Phone = self device; the shared living-room TV = family device. The two primitives compose without overlap.

### 3.3.5 `consent-subject` — `consent_record` subject_kind

The canonical envelope shape when consent is the primary subject of the Contribution itself (parallel to [`key_grant`](#key_grant) and [`takedown_notice`](#takedown_notice) — a ceremony-shape over the underlying primitive). Use cases: standalone partnership grants, DSAR-shape consent declarations, multi-party contracts, explicit consent ceremonies with locked field schemas.

**Both shapes admitted at the same gate**: subject-side consent MAY ride a bare `scores` on `consent:state:*` against any target Contribution (the common case, see [CC 3.3.1](#3.3.1) composition pattern), OR ride this `consent_record` subject_kind when an explicit ceremony envelope is wanted. Per the [CC 2.4](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.4) layering principle, bare `scores` is the primitive; `consent_record` is the ceremony UX shape over the primitive.

```
consent_record {
  subject_key_id: key_id // the subject declaring stance, or on a partnership half the partner, CC 4.4.3.20 (federation_keys
    // OR canonical-hash per CC 2.3.2)
  target_key_id: key_id | null // optional: producer/recipient for bilateral grants
  stance: ConsentStance // closed-set enum per below
  scope: [ConsentScope,...] // open vocab; see CC 3.3.1
  asserted_at: uint // POSIX milliseconds per CC 2.6.2
  valid_until: Option<rfc3339> // null = indefinite
  deletion_sla_days: Option<u32> // for revocations: producer obligation window
    // (composes with `consent:deletion_sla:{days}`)
  decay_protocol: Option<string> // optional: named multi-stage decay path
    // (e.g., "ciris-agent-90day")
  bilateral_pair_id: Option<string> // for bilateral grants: pairs subject + producer
    // Contributions via topical_relation:bilateral_pair
}
```

**ConsentStance** (closed-set):

| value | meaning |
|-----------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| granted | Subject affirms; processing may proceed within scope and valid_until |
| revoked | Subject withdraws; producer must complete deletion within sla window (CC 3.3.1 D1) |
| expired | Substrate emission when valid_until passes without renewal |

**Admission rules.** A `consent_record` Contribution is admitted iff:
1. **Required fields present**: `subject_key_id`, `stance` (closed-set), `asserted_at` (an instant of CC 2.6.2). All others are optional per the envelope above; absent optionals ride the omit rule of [CC 2.6.1.2](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.6.1.2).
2. **`stance` is a closed-set value** (`granted` / `revoked` / `expired`); **`expired` is substrate-emitted only** — a producer/subject MUST NOT assert `expired` (it is the substrate's `valid_until`-passed emission).
3. **Tier eligibility** per [CC 5.3.2.2](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.3.2.2): a `stance: revoked` `consent_record` is **NOT local-tier-eligible** (it carries subject revocation authority over another party's content) — it goes federation-tier (hybrid-signed) or rides the CC 5.3.2.2 24-hour `local → federation` promotion. A `stance: granted` *self*-consent where the subject holds sole authority MAY be local-tier per [CC 5.3.2.5](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.3.2.5).
4. **Composition with the [CC 2.4.1.1](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.4.1.1) `withdraws` gate**: a `stance: revoked` `consent_record` whose `subject_key_id` ∈ the target's `subject_key_ids[]` is admitted under CC 2.4.1.1 subject-revocation authority (rules 2–4). The substrate SHOULD record which rule admitted it (the CC 2.4.1.1 per-rule audit metadata). No producer co-signature and **no quorum** is required — single-subject authority suffices ([CC 4.4.3.29](part_4_composition_governance.md#4.4.3.29)).

It rides the same admission gate as a bare `scores` on `consent:state:*`; the `consent_record` form simply carries the locked payload schema instead of a free dimension.

**Bilateral pair pattern**:

```
1. Subject emits consent_record(subject_key_id: <the producer's key>, stance: granted,
   bilateral_pair_id: <fresh-uuid>) +
   scores on consent:partnership_grant:v1
2. Producer emits consent_record(subject_key_id: <the subject's key>,
   stance: granted, bilateral_pair_id: <same-uuid>) +
   scores on consent:partnership_accept:v1
3. topical_relation:bilateral_pair links the two Contributions
4. Consumer policy treats the partnership as ratified iff both halves present and live
   under the same bilateral_pair_id with stance: granted
```

The structural primitives close the bilateral shape — no new attestation_type, no new envelope field beyond `subject_key_ids` itself.

#### 3.3.5.1 `fair-exchange` — Optimistic fair exchange (worked example, no new primitive)

This worked example states the [CC 1.7](part_1_foundation.md#1.7) in-grammar claim as **normative**. The claim is that accountable ("optimistic") fair exchange — a digital good D traded for a settlement S, with adjudicated recourse — composes entirely from the existing 1+4 set plus the bilateral pair pattern above. The trustless, third-party-free atomic swap (HTLC-class) remains the [CC 1.7](part_1_foundation.md#1.7) standing falsification target; this pattern does **not** reach it. Offeror A and acceptor B exchange across a steward-bound escrow custodian E, with the always-present named-moderator / WA as the optimistic third party invoked only on dispute (WBD applied to exchange).

```
1. OFFER / ACCEPT — bilateral ratification (the CC 3.3.5 bilateral pair above,
   CC 2.3.2.4 consumer-policy ratification):
   A emits consent_record(subject_key_id: B, stance: granted, bilateral_pair_id: X)
     + scores on consent:partnership_grant:v1
   B emits consent_record(subject_key_id: A, stance: granted, bilateral_pair_id: X)
     + scores on consent:partnership_accept:v1
   topical_relation:bilateral_pair links the halves; ratified iff both present and live.

2. DIGITAL LEG — steward-bound escrow custodian (the CC 4.4.3.3 archive_custody
   precedent: a custodian holding per-epoch keys decoupled from the live roster):
   A authorizes E via delegates_to (CC 2.4.1.2) scoped to release-of-D.
   On confirmed S, E emits a key_grant (CC 3.3.2) to B — the release.

3. VALUE LEG — settlement (CC 3.3.10), off-stack on an external rail:
   a settlement attestation binds S to the ratified pair
     (settled_action_ref = the offer/accept Contribution).

4. DISPUTE — optimistic adjudication: absent dispute, parties + E complete
   unilaterally (the optimistic path); on dispute the named-moderator
   (CC 4.5.4) / WA (CC 4.3) adjudicates and a hard_case:* event records it.

5. DEFECTION — accountable recourse: non-delivery composes as a
   commitment_fulfillment (CC 3.1.9.2) shortfall; a proven_rogue
   slashing:{outcome} (CC 3.1.9.2) against staked standing (the CC 2.5 stake
   axis) follows on the slash duty-holder's verdict (CC 4.5.5).
```

**What this buys, and what it does not.** 1+4 buys **accountability, not atomicity**: a malicious or colluding escrow can still defect (after-the-fact redress is not prevention), and a revealed `key_grant` ([CC 3.3.2](#3.3.2)) is forward-only — it cannot be un-revealed. The residual bridges are the value leg ([CC 3.3.10](#3.3.10)) and physical delivery, neither fair-exchange-specific. No new attestation_type and no new envelope field — the [CC 1.7](part_1_foundation.md#1.7) 1+4 lockdown holds.

### 3.3.6 `identity` — `identity_occurrence` subject_kind

The wire-format primitive that lets one logical identity speak across multiple **trusted participants**: a person's devices (phone / laptop / server / embedded), or the keys of one agent's own identity. The `occurrence_id` envelope field ([CC 2.1](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.1)) names which occurrence emitted a Contribution; `identity_occurrence` is the **wire-format binding** that lets the substrate know `key_phone` and `key_laptop` both represent the same identity `key_identity`. This is the integrity foundation under self-scope: it is what makes "this is me, on another device" a cryptographic fact rather than a guess.

Without this primitive: `cohort_scope: self` content cannot reach the user's other devices — the substrate has no structural way to know which keys are co-self. With it: the at-rest encryption flow automatically wraps DEKs to the admitted occurrences that the allow lists of their nodes provide for ([CC 6.1.5.3](part_6_the_coherence_mathematics.md#6.1.5.3)) when new content is admitted at `cohort_scope: self`.

```
identity_occurrence {
  identity_key_id: key_id // root identity (the user's logical identity)
  occurrence_key_id: key_id // this participant's signing key
  device_class: DeviceClass // closed-set enum per below
  hardware_attestation: Option<base64> // TPM / Secure Enclave / StrongBox / SGX
    // etc. attestation blob; null for software-only
  transport_destination: Option<TransportDestination> // Reticulum binding (below)
  encryption_pubkeys: Option<EncryptionPubkeys> // content-KEM keys (CC 3.3.6.1 below);
    // present ⇒ this occurrence is a v2 wrap target
  build_manifest_hash: Option<hex64> // the build this occurrence runs: the hash of the
    // pipeline-signed manifest (CC 3.1.2 provenance:build_manifest)
  build_manifest_ref: Option<uuid> // attestation_id of that provenance:build_manifest:{target} row
  asserted_at: uint // POSIX milliseconds per CC 2.6.2
  valid_until: Option<rfc3339> // null = indefinite
}
```

**The build an occurrence runs (normative).** An occurrence names the build it runs on its own row, by `build_manifest_hash` and `build_manifest_ref`. `build_manifest_hash` is the hash of the pipeline-signed manifest, a byte string ([CC 2.6.1.2](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.6.1.2)). `build_manifest_ref` is the `attestation_id` of the `provenance:build_manifest:{target}` row that manifest is published in ([CC 3.1.2](#3.1.2)). The occurrence supplies them at registration from its verifier's result. The occurrence waits for the provenance row it cites. It counts at a node only where that row is Rooted there and its manifest hash equals `build_manifest_hash`, and otherwise concludes nothing. **A row about a running occurrence resolves its version through the roster:** a reader takes the build from the occurrence row live at the claim's `asserted_at`, never from a version string the claim's producer asserts. A row with both members absent names no build.

**EncryptionPubkeys**:

| field | type | meaning |
|----------------------|-----------|----------------------------------------------------------------|
| x25519_base64 | [u8; 32] | classical KEM half — a FRESH content-KEM key (NOT the signing |
| | | key, NOT the transport x25519 below — see key-separation) |
| ml_kem_768_base64 | [u8; 1184] | PQC KEM half (FIPS 203, ML-KEM-768; exactly 1184 raw bytes — `ML_KEM_768_PUBKEY_LEN` — pre-base64) |

**TransportDestination**:

| field | type | meaning |
|---------------------------|-----------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| reticulum_x25519_pubkey | [u8; 32] | transport identity's encryption key |
| reticulum_ed25519_pubkey | [u8; 32] | transport identity's signing key |
| destination_hash | [u8; 16] | RNS destination hash; MUST derive from the two pubkeys |
| | | + app_name + aspects per the CC 3.3.6.3 algorithm |
| app_name | string | RNS destination app (e.g. "ciris.federation") |
| aspects | [string] | RNS aspects (ordered; part of the hash preimage) |

**DeviceClass** (closed-set):

| value | scope |
|------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
| phone | Mobile device (iOS / Android / etc.); typically hardware-rooted |
| laptop | Personal computing device (macOS / Linux / Windows) |
| server | Always-on infrastructure node (home server, VPS, etc.) |
| embedded | IoT / hardware peripheral / signing dongle |
| agent | An AI agent's own key, under that agent's own identity only |
| service | Background service / scheduled job / API integration acting |
| | on the identity's behalf |

**Admission is roster maintenance.** An `identity_occurrence` row is signed by a live roster key of the identity (the genesis key or any admitted occurrence) and lands under the two-path policy of [CC 3.3.6.4](#3.3.6.4). It also carries the occurrence key's own statement over the same payload, its proof of possession, so no roster binds a key its signer does not hold. A row that lacks it waits for it ([CC 2.6.1.9](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.6.1.9)). Higher-assurance setups MAY layer requirements on `hardware_attestation` via consumer policy ([CC 4.5.12.3](part_4_composition_governance.md#4.5.12.3)).

**Revocation**: an eviction is a `withdraws` against the `identity_occurrence` row, proposed by a live roster key and landing under [CC 3.3.6.4](#3.3.6.4). No single occurrence evicts at once with no window: that unilateral configuration is one a thief wins in two steps. Once it lands the substrate stops wrapping new key_grants to the evicted key; DEKs delivered before it lands are out of scope per the [CC 4.4.3.22](part_4_composition_governance.md#4.4.3.22) forward-secrecy rule.

**Cardinality**: an identity MAY admit unbounded occurrences; the substrate carries no hard cap (operator policy MAY impose per-deployment limits). When a new occurrence is admitted, substrate emits `hard_case:identity_occurrence_added` ([CC 3.4.3](part_3_the_namespace.md#3.4.3)) so consumer policy can observe membership growth.

**Composition with a CEG-native agent**: an agent's occurrence binds the agent's own identity, and its owner authors it ([CC 2.4.1.1](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.4.1.1), [CC 2.6.1.7](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.6.1.7)). An agent key never signs as its owner. An occurrence that places a `node` or `agent` key under a `user` or `accord_holder` identity, or the reverse, concludes nothing, `occurrence_mixes_person_and_machine`.

#### 3.3.6.1 `encryption_pubkeys` — the recipient content-encryption KEM binding

The [CC 5.2](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.2) at-rest DEK cascade is **substrate-wraps-by-default**: the substrate generates the per-write DEK and wraps it to each active recipient. That wrap (`wrap_algorithm: v2`, CC 3.3.2) needs each recipient's **x25519 + ML-KEM-768 encryption** keys — but the federation directory's key registration carries only **signing** keys (Ed25519 + ML-DSA-65), and **ML-KEM cannot be derived from ML-DSA** (independent algorithms). So recipients must register encryption keys, and the substrate must resolve them by `key_id`. `encryption_pubkeys` is that binding.

**The binding rides `identity_occurrence`, exactly parallel to `transport_destination`.** It inherits the same four properties, already enforced, that an encryption-key binding requires:
1. **Self-certified** — admitted only when `attesting_key_id == identity_key_id` (or a current occurrence of it), so "these are identity K's encryption keys" is cryptographically proven, not trust-on-first-use. A spoofer cannot forge it.
2. **Composite-signed** ([CC 2.6.1.7](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.6.1.7)) — the binding itself is PQC-signed.
3. **Rotatable via `supersedes`** — a new `identity_occurrence` superseding the prior rotates the KEM keys **without touching the stable signing `key_id`** that anchors every attestation/grant. A compromised ML-KEM key rotates for forward secrecy; the signing identity is untouched. (Bundling these onto the signing key registration would couple two independent rotation lifecycles — the reason this is NOT a field on the key record.)
4. **Already cross-region replicated** — `identity_occurrence` is its own kind in the locked replication wire, so the encryption pubkeys propagate inside the occurrence envelope that already replicates — **no new replication kind, no Edge wire change**. A cross-region recipient's keys resolve wherever its occurrence has propagated. An occurrence travels to the audience its owner placed it at ([CC 5.4.6](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.4.6)). Where that audience is `federation` it replicates in cleartext, as a signing key does.

**Key separation (normative — never reuse, and admission-enforced).** The `x25519` here is a **fresh content-KEM key**, distinct from BOTH (a) the occurrence's signing keys AND (b) the Reticulum transport x25519 in [CC 3.3.6.2](#3.3.6.2) `destination_hash = hash(x25519 ‖ ed25519)`. The transport x25519 of (b) is the *RET-link* transport key, classical-only — the federation seed never enters the transport layer, and the transport key never wraps content DEKs. Three key *purposes* — signing, RET-transport, content-KEM — are three distinct keypairs. Deriving the content-KEM x25519 from either of the others is a conformance violation (cross-protocol key reuse). **Admission check:** when an `identity_occurrence` carries BOTH `encryption_pubkeys` AND `transport_destination`, the substrate MUST **reject at admission** if `encryption_pubkeys.x25519_base64` decodes to the same 32 bytes as `transport_destination.reticulum_x25519_pubkey` — the one reuse case that is wire-checkable for free. Reuse of the *signing* key as KEM key is not byte-comparable on the wire — different algorithms — and remains a producer-side conformance obligation. The bindings of a private room ([CC 3.1.3.2](#3.1.3.2)) are a fourth purpose and take a fourth keypair, which is never the content-KEM pair. Its public key is `room_binding_xwing_pubkey`, a top-level member of the occurrence beside `encryption_pubkeys`: an X-Wing public key of exactly 1216 bytes. The reuse refusals read its halves, bytes 0..1184 and bytes 1184..1216. A half equal to either half of `encryption_pubkeys`, of `transit_xwing_pubkey` or of `onion_hop_xwing_pubkey` on the same row, or to the transport x25519, is refused. The token is `room_binding_ml_kem_768_reuse` for the first half and `room_binding_x25519_reuse` for the second. The binding key is also never the `kem_xwing_pubkey` of a room key. No door compares those two, since the comparison would tie the room key to the identity, so that separation is the producer's.

**Forward-secrecy scope.** KEM-key rotation via `supersedes` bounds **future** exposure only: grants wrapped *after* rotation use the new key. Rotation does **nothing** for history. Every `key_grant` wrapped to the compromised key before the rotation persists at rest. The at-rest threat model ([CC 5.2](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.2) disk-forensics / host-operator adversary) is *precisely* an adversary holding those old grant bytes. With the old private key that adversary decrypts every DEK ever wrapped to that key, and rotation does not revoke bytes the adversary already holds. **Recovering historical content after a KEM-key compromise requires DEK rotation + content re-encryption under the new DEK — which CEG does NOT mandate.** This is a named gap (the [CC 1.13.3](part_1_foundation.md#1.13.3) honesty discipline). Operators with a compromised-key event MUST treat all content whose DEKs were wrapped to that key as exposed, and MAY re-encrypt. The spec provides the mechanism (new DEK + new grants + `supersedes`) but no automatic trigger. Do not represent KEM rotation as recovering the confidentiality of content wrapped before it.

**These feed `wrap_algorithm: v2` directly.** `{x25519, ml_kem_768}` are precisely the recipient inputs to `x25519_mlkem768_aes256_gcm_hkdf_sha256` ([CC 3.3.2](#3.3.2)). A consumer/substrate resolving a recipient's wrap target reads the **current (non-superseded, within-`valid_until`) `identity_occurrence` for that `key_id` → its `encryption_pubkeys`**.

**Fail-secure conformance (the [CC 5.2](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.2) tie-in).** Because CC 5.2 *mandates* v2 for at-rest encryption, a recipient whose current occurrence carries **no valid ML-KEM-768 key is fail-secure *excluded* from the grant**. The content stays encrypted and unreachable to that recipient; the substrate MUST NOT fall back to plaintext or to v1. To be an at-rest-encryption recipient, an identity MUST have an `identity_occurrence` carrying `encryption_pubkeys` that the sealer holds. (This also resolves the "`family` member named only by `key_id` with no occurrence" case: no presence ⇒ no wrap target ⇒ excluded. That is correct, since there would be nowhere to deliver/store the wrapped DEK for a member that never established a presence.)

**1+4 preserved** — `encryption_pubkeys` is one optional field-set on the existing `identity_occurrence` subject_kind ([CC 3.3](#3.3) mechanism; no new subject_kind, no new replication kind). Fifteenth path ([CC 1.7](part_1_foundation.md#1.7)) — the wire format expresses **its own at-rest-encryption key layer** (recipient KEM-key resolution for substrate-wraps) by composition.

#### 3.3.6.2 `transport-authenticated` — `transport_destination` — the authenticated identity↔address binding

This entry says how a node learns, with proof, which network address belongs to which identity. In a **CEG/RET stack there is no DNS**: a node resolves a community member to a *reachable address* with no trusted nameserver. The `transport_destination` field is the wire-format primitive that makes that resolution **authenticated** instead of trust-on-first-use. Integrity at the addressing layer: you can prove who you are routing to. Among other things, the entry also sets the transit KEX pair and the onion hop key that ride the same binding, and the marker by which a node opts out of relaying.

**The layer split it closes.** A node's Reticulum destination is a *dedicated dual-key transport identity* `hash(x25519 ‖ ed25519)`. It is deliberately **separate** from the federation signing key (the federation seed never enters the node's transport substrate). So "destination D belongs to federation key K" is a claim that must be *proven*, not assumed. A bare Reticulum announce only proves the announcer controls *that transport identity*, not that it legitimately belongs to K (any peer can announce `key_id=registry-steward-us` paired with an adversary destination → senders route to the adversary).

**The binding = a federation-key-signed `identity_occurrence` carrying `transport_destination`.** The occurrence is admitted only when `attesting_key_id == identity_key_id` (or a current occurrence of it), and it carries the composite signature ([CC 2.6.1.7](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.6.1.7)). So the binding `destination_hash ← identity` is cryptographically authenticated. A spoofer cannot forge an `identity_occurrence` signed by the real key. This makes the signed-announce attestation a **first-class, federation-wide, auditable CEG shape**. The directory holds it as the durable source of truth, and the announce app-data MAY carry it for self-authenticating discovery. An owned node's route is the exception: its owner hands it, or a referral does, and no forwarder serves it ([CC 5.4.6](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.4.6)).

**Conformance**: a Consumer resolving a member's address MUST verify:

- (1) the `identity_occurrence` signature against the member's federation key;
- (2) that `destination_hash` recomputes from `reticulum_x25519_pubkey`, `reticulum_ed25519_pubkey`, `app_name`, and `aspects` per the **[CC 3.3.6.3](#3.3.6.3)** pinned algorithm (no free-floating hash); and
- (3) the occurrence is non-superseded + within `valid_until` at resolution time.

An unauthenticated announce (no matching signed `transport_destination`) is **advisory-only**: usable as a routing hint, never as an authorization. Rotating the Reticulum destination (new transport identity) is a new `identity_occurrence` `supersedes`-ing the prior: location changes without touching federation identity or community membership. A seated serve node is the exception: the accord holders re-bind its destination and transit pair by a cosigned `transport:canonical_rebind:v1` row ([CC 3.1.3](#3.1.3)). It is counted at a strict majority of the holders of the bundle in force, or a later bundle re-seats the node ([CC 4.2.1](part_4_composition_governance.md#4.2.1)). Its own rotation counts only after a re-bind has landed; before that, no node counts it (`serve_transit_pair_rotation_before_rebind`).

**The transit KEX binding (normative).** A node that relays carries one **transit public key** `transit_xwing_pubkey` on this `transport_destination` binding: exactly 1216 bytes, the X-Wing public key `pk_M ‖ pk_X`, the ML-KEM-768 encapsulation key of 1184 bytes then the X25519 key of 32 bytes. It carries the key with the four properties of [CC 3.3.6.1](#3.3.6.1): attester = the identity, hybrid-signed, rotatable via `supersedes` without touching the signing `key_id`, replicated inside the occurrence envelope.

**A seat's transit key (normative).** A seated serve node's transit key is first the one its binding in the genesis bundle carries ([CC 5.3.4](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.3.4)), and it moves only by `transport:canonical_rebind`, counted by the accord's holders. A binding of this form carries `transit_xwing_pubkey` only. A node of this form takes a seat's `transit_xwing_pubkey` from the bundle or from such a re-bind, and a seat's own binding that carries another key is not honoured.

**The binding's members (normative).** The binding is a row of the family `identity:occurrence`, authored and signed by the identity it binds. Its payload carries these members, each at its top level ([CC 2.6.1.4](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.6.1.4)):

| Member | Type | Required when |
|---|---|---|
| `transport_destination` | a map of exactly five members, no more: `reticulum_x25519_pubkey`, `reticulum_ed25519_pubkey`, `app_name`, `aspects` and `destination_hash` ([CC 3.3.6.3](#3.3.6.3)) | always |
| `transit_xwing_pubkey` | 1216 bytes, beside `transport_destination` | on a node that relays, and on every seat |
| `onion_hop_xwing_pubkey` | 1216 bytes, beside `transport_destination` | on a node that relays, and on every serve node |
| `onion_relay` | exactly the map `{"opt_out": true}`, or absent | on a node that opts out of relaying |
| `refs` | the node's own key record, by row id under the `also` role `cites` | on a seat's binding |

**Key separation is normative and admission-enforced**: the transit pair is distinct from the signing keys, from the content KEM keys of 3.3.6.1, and from the Reticulum link x25519 above. A binding that reuses any of them is refused.

**Scope of the admission check:** admission enforces the separation **in-row**, the transit pair against every key carried on the same signed row. Those keys are the RNS link x25519, the transport ed25519, the signer's pinned key, and the content KEM keys of 3.3.6.1 when they ride this row. That is exactly as 3.3.6.1 scopes its own check. Separation from keys carried on a *different* row (the content KEM keys of 3.3.6.1 when they ride a separate occurrence row) is the **producer's duty**. That is because an admission verdict that depended on which row arrived first would differ between nodes holding the same rows ([CC 3.2](#3.2) T8 vii).

**What a dialler may seal to.** An initiator opens a sealed link ([CC 5.3.3.10](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.3.3.10) E1) only to a transit pair authenticated to the identity it means to reach:

- this binding, hybrid-signed by that identity and passing the in-row separation, from whatever source it was obtained;
- a Rooted binding; or
- the pairing pin of [CC 3.2](#3.2) adding a device (f).

**Rooted standing is not required to seal.** It governs what the peer may be served ([CC 3.2](#3.2) T8). A not-yet-Rooted sealed link carries the bootstrap kinds, the allegiance rows and the pairing plane. It also carries rows addressed to the peer and the rows a bounded cohort delivers to it as a member ([CC 5.3.4](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.3.4)). So two peers who hold each other's signed bindings seal and root each other with no canonical in the path.

**A bare or unsigned announce never supplies a pair.** A dialler holding none fetches this row by the pre-seal route request of [CC 5.3.3.10](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.3.3.10) E1, verifies it, and seals. It falls back to the pairing pin only where no responder can be reached.

**The cross-row case** is closed at use, not at admission. A consumer that resolves a relay's transit pair and finds it equal to any key on the identity's current occurrence treats the node as carrying **no valid transit pair** (it cannot relay). That verdict is deterministic over the fold and never over arrival order, with no retraction row.

**The key that binds a non-member relay** in the [CC 5.3.3.10](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.3.3.10) E1 hop-by-hop hybrid KEX is this pair: the relay's published static pair against the initiator's ephemeral hybrid key inside the link's first exchange. The static half binds the relay to its identity, and the ephemeral half gives per-link freshness. Pattern, label, info layout and rotation cadence are the verifier's.

**What does not bind a relay.** A KeyPackage init key is refused as a hop key (it is a cohort credential, and a relay holds no cohort secret, E1 and [CC 5.4.6](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.4.6)). An ephemeral-only exchange is insufficient on its own (the relay would be authenticated only by the classical RNS link proof, which E1 forbids).

**A node whose current occurrence carries no valid transit pair cannot relay** (fail-secure, as 3.3.6.1 excludes a recipient with no ML-KEM key). A consumer resolves a peer's KEX pubkeys from this signed binding and never from a bare announce.

**1+4 preserved**: one optional field-set on the existing binding, no new subject_kind, no new replication kind.

**The onion hop key (normative).** A relaying node, and every serve node, carries a static **X-Wing onion hop public key** `onion_hop_xwing_pubkey` on this `transport_destination` binding. Each carries it with the same four properties as the transit pair: attester = the identity, hybrid-signed, rotatable via `supersedes` without touching the signing `key_id`, replicated inside the occurrence envelope. The hop key is the key an onion packet's layer for this hop is encapsulated to ([CC 5.4.6](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.4.6)).

**Key separation is normative and admission-enforced in-row exactly as for the transit pair**: the hop key is distinct from the transit pair and from every other key on the same signed row. A binding that reuses one is refused. Separation from keys on a different row is the producer's duty. A consumer that finds the hop key equal to any key on the identity's current occurrence treats the node as carrying no valid hop key.

**A node with no valid hop key cannot relay onion traffic.** A node that has opted out of relaying carries none. A serve node with none does not conform to [CC 5.4.6](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.4.6).

**The opt-out marker (normative).** A node that opts out of relaying for others ([CC 5.4.6](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.4.6)) carries `"onion_relay": { "opt_out": true }` in the signed envelope of this binding. The marker is hybrid-signed like the rest of the row and absent by default. The node withdraws its hop key on the same superseding row. The marker takes the node out of the layer deal, and the absent key makes a stale route through it impossible.

A serve seat carrying the marker is out of conformance (`seat_opted_out`). Which node may opt out and which may not is the rule of [CC 5.4.6](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.4.6).

**The marker is explicit** because an absent hop key alone is ambiguous. It could mean opted out, not yet capable, a key not yet minted, or a seat in violation, and the register, the client and the conformance witnesses tell those apart.

**The hop key's shape (normative).** The member `onion_hop_xwing_pubkey` is one byte string ([CC 2.6.1.2](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.6.1.2)) of exactly 1216 bytes, the X-Wing public key `pk_M ‖ pk_X`: the ML-KEM-768 encapsulation key of 1184 bytes, then the X25519 key of 32 bytes. Its earlier form is [CC 8.11.20](part_8_appendices.md#8.11.20).

**It lives in the signed envelope only, never in a typed column**, so the row's content hash does not depend on a store's projection.

**What is refused.** A key of the wrong length is refused as malformed, under the same rule as the transit key. The reuse refusals read the key's halves, bytes 0..1184 and bytes 1184..1216. A half equal to either half of `transit_xwing_pubkey`, to either half of `encryption_pubkeys` on the same row, to the transport x25519 or ed25519, or to the signer's pinned keys is refused. The token is `onion_hop_ml_kem_768_reuse` for the first half and `onion_hop_x25519_reuse` for the second.

#### 3.3.6.3 `rns` — RNS destination-hash algorithm (pinned)

This is a **two-stage** hash — it is **NOT** a single SHA-256 over a flat `x25519 ‖ ed25519 ‖ app_name ‖ aspects` preimage. The naive flat form yields a *different, wrong* value, so the algorithm is pinned exactly below for independent recompute.

Pinned constants (SHA-256 throughout — RNS `full_hash`):

| name | value | RNS origin |
|---|---|---|
| `NAME_HASH_LEN` | **10** bytes | `Identity.NAME_HASH_LENGTH` = 80 bits |
| `DEST_HASH_LEN` | **16** bytes | `Reticulum.TRUNCATED_HASHLENGTH` = 128 bits |

Algorithm:

```
# 1. Expanded name — UTF-8. app_name, then each aspect dot-joined, IN THE FIELD ORDER.
# The identity hexhash is NOT included (RNS computes name_hash with identity=None).
expanded_name = app_name
for aspect in aspects: # `aspects` in the field's given order
  reject if "." in aspect # dots are illegal inside an aspect
  expanded_name += "." + aspect

# 2. name_hash = first 10 bytes of SHA-256(expanded_name)
name_hash = SHA256(utf8(expanded_name))[:NAME_HASH_LEN] # 10 bytes

# 3. identity_hash = first 16 bytes of SHA-256(x25519_pub ‖ ed25519_pub)
# Key order is reticulum_x25519_pubkey (32) THEN reticulum_ed25519_pubkey (32) —
# RNS get_public_key = pub_bytes (X25519) ‖ sig_pub_bytes (Ed25519).
identity_hash = SHA256(reticulum_x25519_pubkey ‖ reticulum_ed25519_pubkey)[:DEST_HASH_LEN] # 16 bytes

# 4. destination_hash = first 16 bytes of SHA-256(name_hash ‖ identity_hash)
# addr_hash_material is the 26-byte concat (10 + 16); final hash truncates to 16.
destination_hash = SHA256(name_hash ‖ identity_hash)[:DEST_HASH_LEN] # 16 bytes
```

**Pinned source**: the Reticulum reference implementation's destination-hash and identity routines (`full_hash` = SHA-256; `truncated_hash`; the public key = `pub_bytes ‖ sig_pub_bytes`; `TRUNCATED_HASHLENGTH = 128`). **CEG owns this reproduction**: it is the closed conformance source and does **not** float with upstream Reticulum — a future upstream hash change is a deliberate CEG version bump, never silent drift. A verifier that recomputes `destination_hash` per the four steps above and compares for byte-equality has performed the destination-authenticity check; a mismatch MUST be treated as an unauthenticated (advisory-only) announce.

**1+4 preserved** — `transport_destination` is one optional field on the existing `identity_occurrence` subject_kind ([CC 3.3](#3.3) mechanism; no new subject_kind). Twelfth path ([CC 1.7](part_1_foundation.md#1.7)) — the wire format expresses **its own addressing layer** (DNS-free, self-certifying member resolution) by composition.

#### 3.3.6.4 `self-roster` — The key roster of a self: one fedID, its keys, who may act and how the roster changes (normative)

This entry sets out the key roster of a self: one fedID, its keys, who may act and how the roster changes. It also says what the self-roster model checks.

**One self, one string.** A self is one fedID ([CC 2.6.8](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.6.8)): one person, one `key_id` string, the same on every device. It is what owner-bindings, occurrences, contacts and a shared identity code name. The keys that may sign as that self are its **roster**: the `identity_occurrence` rows under `identity_key_id`. Each roster key lives on one node and a node holds at most one roster key of a given self; the node's own key is a different key ([CC 3.4.7.3](#3.4.7.3)). The genesis key is roster key one and nothing more: the fedID's fingerprint is derived from it. The string survives as the self's name if that key is later evicted, and resolution then verifies the roster chain back to it.

**On the wire:** the genesis key's eviction is an `identity_occurrence` revocation of the pair (fedID, fedID) signed by another live roster key, landing under the two paths below. The genesis key revoking that pair itself retires its transport self-occurrence and evicts nothing. An evicted genesis key is not re-established by a later assertion of the pair, and the fedID string keeps naming the self. A revocation of the pair that carries no roster-door vote does not evict.

**Naming a roster key.** A roster key other than the genesis key is named `<fedID>-<fingerprint>`. The whole fedID string is the [CC 2.6.8](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.6.8) label. The fingerprint is the first ten lowercase base32 characters of SHA-256 over the key's *own* raw Ed25519 public key. The name is the 2.6.8 form exactly, verifiable against its own key. It carries no device name (the node key carries that). It cannot be read as another person, because the genesis fingerprint is inside it. Two spellings are refused: a device-derived id (`device-<hex>-<fp>`), and `<label>-<own fingerprint>` with the bare label, which reads as a second fedID. The 2.6.8 rule that a consumer verifies a `key_id`'s fingerprint against the public key it obtains holds for the genesis key for the fedID itself and for each roster key for its own id. A consumer MUST NOT treat a roster key id as a different identity.

**Authority of a roster key.** Any live roster key signs *as the fedID* for every owner act ([CC 2.7.5](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.7.5)): consent, an owner-binding and its widening, root acceptance ([CC 3.2](#3.2)), the self room, contacts, and approving the next device. Nothing is reserved to the genesis key. A special genesis key would be a single point of loss, which contradicts the invariant below. A gate that asks whether the author is the owner or steward MUST accept a live roster key of the same fedID at the row's signed `asserted_at`, not only the key named on the binding. That `asserted_at` is bounded by the past-freshness window W of the admitting substrate (`asserted_at_stale`), so an evicted key can backdate an owner act into its old live window by at most W, and no further. That bound is the same one the consent fold puts on a backdated grant ([CC 2.6.7](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.6.7)). In a private room ([CC 3.1.3.2](#3.1.3.2)) no roster key signs. Each device holds its own room key in the person's voice and makes its own bindings. A further room key is seated by the room keys of that voice already live there, and its seat row commits to the same person.

**The bound applies only to a key that has lost standing:** W is checked when the author key is not a live roster key of the self *at receipt* — evicted, revoked, or never seated. A row signed by a key that is still live admits at any age, so a new device syncing a self's history admits its legitimate old rows. That is because the backdating threat exists only for a key that has lost standing.

**Maintenance: the two paths.** An addition or an eviction is a proposal signed by a live roster key; one open proposal per proposer. With **two or more** live keys it lands by either path:

| Path | What lands the proposal |
|---|---|
| The **quorum path** | a strict majority of the live roster, proposer counted, approves and it lands at once |
| The **lone path** | the window `W_self` = 86 400 s elapses and no strict majority of the *other* members objects, and for an eviction the target was silent all window (any signed act by a roster key answers every open proposal and proves the key is not lost) |

A vote from an evicted key is void.

**The proposer's own withdrawal (normative).** The proposer MAY withdraw its own open proposal, an addition or an eviction, since the proposal is its own row ([CC 2.4.1.1](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.4.1.1) rule 1). The withdrawal is the proposer's own voice, on a clause of its own, and it is read after the majority's approval. An approval that is met stands against a withdrawal. A withdrawal with no majority approved gives `refused` at once. An approval that has the withdrawal in its past approves nothing. The proposer's approval by opening still counts toward a majority that formed. A withdrawal signed by any other key is no voice. A lone landing that states `landed` with the withdrawal in its past concludes nothing. A withdrawal concurrent with a lone landing is recounted with it, and the proposal is then contested ([CC 2.7](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.7), the window). A withdrawal that names the landing came after it and changes nothing. A landed eviction is a revocation, and nobody withdraws it.

**The lone path is a window of rows (normative).** A roster change binds others. So the lone path closes by a signed row and never by a node's own clock ([CC 2.7](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.7), the window). The window's opener is the proposal. Its other two rows are of the family `window:{state}` ([CC 3.1.3](#3.1.3)).

*The held row.* A roster key signs a `window:held` row to say that it holds the proposal. The row names the proposal in `refs.target`, and it MAY name other rows. It names no head, and it names no row in `refs.prev`. A held row MUST NOT have in its past a row the proposal's target signed, other than what the proposal has in its own past. One that does is no held row, and a landing that names it concludes nothing. Its `asserted_at` is the instant from which that key counts the window. A held row is not a receipt ([CC 2.7](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.7)), and it keeps no act in force.

*The landing.* The same key signs a `window:landed` or a `window:refused` row, and that row is the landing. It names the proposal in `refs.target` and its signer's own held row in `refs.prev`. It names every row it counted in `refs.also.cites`, and it names no head. The row under `refs.prev` MUST be a `window:held` row of the same proposal by the landing's own signer, and otherwise the landing concludes nothing. The window has elapsed when the landing's `asserted_at` less the held row's `asserted_at` is at least `W_self`. With either instant missing it has not elapsed. No instant of one signer is compared with another's.

*Who concludes.* Any key seated in the roster at the head the proposal names MAY sign a held row and a landing. The proposer may, and so may the target of an eviction. One key signs each row, and no second signer signs it. A landing by any other key concludes nothing.

*A count that is met.* A count that is met needs no clock and no concluder. A strict majority of the roster approving gives `landed` at once, the proposer counted. A strict majority of the others objecting gives `refused` at once. Neither needs a landing row. One signer that answers both ways says nothing.

*What a landing concludes.* A landing concludes only where the outcome it states is the one the policy gives over the landing's own past. The answers counted are the answers in that past. Short of both counts, there is no outcome until the window has elapsed. An eviction is then `refused` where the target signed any row that is in the landing's past and not in the held row's past. Otherwise the proposal is `landed`. A landing that states another outcome concludes nothing, for every reader and in every arrival order.

*Recount.* An answer concurrent with a landing is counted with the landing's past, and so is a row the target of an eviction signed ([CC 2.7](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.7), the window). The landing stands only if the policy still gives the outcome it stated. A row signed by a key whose seat was ended is counted only where the row that ended the seat has it in its past. An answer that names the landing came after it and changes nothing. A second landing names the earlier landing and the late row among the rows it counted. A held row and a landing are never withdrawn, and only a later landing that names a landing answers it.

*The outcome.* A proposal is **open** while no count is met and no landing of it has concluded. Where a count is met and no landing has concluded, the proposal is landed or refused as the count gives. Where a landing has concluded, the proposal is **contested** while no landing stands, or while two landings that stand state different outcomes. Otherwise it is landed or refused, as the landing that stands states. While a proposal is open or contested, nothing it would change has changed. The target of an eviction stays seated, and the key of an addition is not seated. A client shows a lone-path proposal as open, contested, landed or refused.

*What the lone path costs.* Four costs are stated so a person knows them.

- A lone landing is never final against a roster key that can still sign. An answer that leaves the landing unnamed is recounted against it.
- The window's length is the concluder's own word. A thief holding one key can sign the proposal, the held row and the landing at once, with instants a day apart. What stops the thief is any row the owner signs, and never the clock.
- An absent owner looks lost. A reader offered only the thief's rows reads the eviction as landed.
- An owner with one live key cannot evict a stolen key whose holder signs any row.

*An addition.* An addition has the eviction's table without the target's silence. While it is open or contested, the key is not seated. One objection of two others does not stop a lone addition. So a holder of one key of three adds a key after the window, unless both other keys object. At any size, only a strict majority of the others refuses it. That is weaker than the eviction, where any row of the target refuses.

**Three readings the model fixes.**

- The window is measured between two instants of one key, its held row's and its landing's, and never from the proposer's signed `asserted_at`. So a lone-path landing is a signed row that every node reads alike.
- Both thresholds are counted over the roster the proposal names. A proposal made on a roster that has since changed is signed again on the roster as it stands at that signing, so a second eviction is never held to the roster the first one changed.

**The head a self-roster row names.** Every `identity:occurrence` and `identity:occurrence_revocation` names in `refs.head` the last landed self-roster row its signer stood on, a bind or an eviction. The first bind of a new identity names the genesis key's own record. An eviction carries the proof of its signers: it cites each voice's key record and, where that key is bound by an occurrence, the occurrence ([CC 2.6.1.7](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.6.1.7)). Those rows are among its ancestors, so a node that serves or carries the eviction serves them with it ([CC 2.7.5](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.7.5)). A row that merges tips names the others in `refs.further_heads`, as a roster version does ([CC 2.7.8](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.7.8)). The roster at a set of heads is the genesis key, plus every landed bind, less every landed eviction reachable from any head named. Both thresholds are counted over it. A row waits while a head it names is not held.

A row naming a head of which the reader has acknowledged a successor is a sibling. It is void for that reader, and never lands a change by a count over that head ([CC 2.7.8](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.7.8)). A merge names every tip the reader has acknowledged. A reader that has acknowledged nothing reads such a row as one tip among several, and its roster is the fold of the tips ([CC 2.7.8](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.7.8)). So a stolen genesis key that names the genesis head moves no reader that has acknowledged a later bind; a reader with no acknowledgement of its own is the residual of [CC 2.7.9](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.7.9). A model checks each of these rules against a plant.
- The door is a person's: it governs the roster of a user fedID. A node holds one key ([CC 3.4.7.3](#3.4.7.3)) and an agent's occurrence is single-signer, and neither runs these paths. Single-signer means one authorising signer: the bound key's own statement is its proof of possession, never a second authority ([CC 3.3.6](#3.3.6)).

**A self states no end of its own.** A `user` key record MUST NOT state `valid_until` ([CC 2.4.1.1](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.4.1.1)), since no person loses their self to a clock. A roster key's occurrence MAY state an end ([CC 3.3.6.2](#3.3.6.2)), and any live roster key renews it. A device's own node key is a `node` key and ends by its own record. The roster key on that device does not end with it.

*The votes and the policy.* Votes travel on `objection:{state}` ([CC 3.1.9.2](#3.1.9.2): `objection:assent:v1` and `objection:raised:v1`; an answer carries `cohort` = `self`, `cohort_key_id` and `grounds`, and names the proposal in `refs.answers`). The proposal is the proposer's own occurrence or revocation row, named by its row id. The policy is two rows of the governance table ([CC 4.5.13](part_4_composition_governance.md#4.5.13), `self_roster_add`, `self_roster_evict`): enact a strict majority, cancel a strict majority of the others, floor one key, window 86 400 s. This is the one roster where a floor of one voice is right, because every key is the same person's. The same policy as the constitutional halt ([CC 4.2.1.1](part_4_composition_governance.md#4.2.1.1)): one actor's act, a window, the standing set deciding whether it stands.

*One key and two keys.* At **one** key the addition is unilateral: the owner's approval of the device that is joining, which is the add-device flow. At **two** keys the quorum path is both keys and the lone path is the other key's silence. So an honest pair lands at once, and a theft of one of two is a stalemate (each side objects to the other's eviction and the thief can block an addition). Safety holds through that stalemate, and nothing resolves it on the wire. That bound is stated so a person knows it: a self SHOULD hold three keys.

**What the self-roster model (pinned by the register) checks.** The model shows this, case by case:

| Case | What the model shows |
|---|---|
| Three keys, one stolen | the policy closes |
| Three keys, two lost | the policy closes |
| Four keys, one stolen and one lost | the policy closes |
| One key, an addition | the one-key addition lands at once |
| One key, stolen | the loss of the self (`Inv_SelfSurvives` fails, the stated bound) |
| Two keys, one lost | closes |
| Two keys, one stolen | stalls (safety holds, recovery does not) |
| A stolen genesis key naming the genesis head | void for a reader that acknowledged a later bind (the model of the head a row names) |
| A merge of a tip that evicted a key and one that did not | the key stays evicted (the model of the head a row names) |

The stolen device ranges over every member, the genesis key included. The unilateral door fails in two steps. Quorum alone cannot recover two lost keys. The lone path alone never evicts a thief who keeps using the device.

Residuals named rather than closed:

- an owner absent for a whole window looks lost;
- one stolen and one lost of three is a tie;
- two stolen of four is a stalemate;

- a stolen key not yet evicted dates its rows at any instant, because W binds only a key that has lost standing.

### 3.3.7 `consent-directed` — `consent:replication` — directed federation-peer replication consent

This entry says how a node records its consent to replicate a class of its own attestations to one named peer node. Among other things it gives the row's shape, what the row does not enforce, how the grant is revoked and paired, and the cohort allow list an owner's grant may carry.

`consent:replication` is a **member of the [CC 3.3.1](#3.3.1) `consent:*` family, open in its parameters** ([CC 4.5.1.1](part_4_composition_governance.md#4.5.1.1) discipline). It is **not a new structural primitive** (the 1+4 surface is frozen; this rides the existing `scores` attestation_type and adds no envelope field). It names a consent shape the rest of the family does not. The shape is a fabric **node's** standing grant to replicate a class of its own attestations to a **named peer node**, as distinct from a **subject's** consent over a target Contribution.

**The problem it solves.** Cross-node propagation is governed by [CC 4.4.3.4 / CC 5.2](part_5_transport_substrate.md) `cohort_scope`. A node **inside** a community (e.g. the [CC 3.2](#3.2) / [CC 8.1](part_8_appendices.md#8.1) `ciris-canonical` infrastructure community) shares with co-members by community-cohort membership. No per-peer object is needed. A node **outside** that group has no membership edge to ride. So an out-of-group peering needs an **explicit, auditable, revocable** consent object. Concrete case: an in-group lens node replicating `capacity:*` to an out-of-group monitoring node, which replicates its [`observation:reachability:v1`](part_8_appendices.md#8.1.3) rows back. `consent:replication` is that object.

**Shape.** The grant is a bare `scores` Contribution on the dimension **`consent:replication:{version}`** (canonical `consent:replication:v1`). It carries `attesting_key_id = G` (the granting node), and the recipient peer is named in `subject_key_ids[] = [P]`. It is standing (not bound to a target Contribution). It is hybrid-signed and admitted **federation-tier** (it authorizes cross-node flow — not local-tier-eligible, [CC 5.3.2.2](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.3.2.2) discipline). It carries `cohort_scope: federation` (the grant itself is a public governance record). A grant that an unannounced node signs or is named in is never placed at `federation` ([CC 5.4.6](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.4.6)); it is held by the two nodes and no other.

```
scores {
  // ── envelope-level (CC 2.1 table — frozen surface, untouched) ──
  attesting_key_id: G, // the granting (sending) node
  dimension: "consent:replication:v1",
  score: <score>, // within the row's declared polarity (signed, CC 3.1.5); a withdraws/recants retracts, never a score value
  subject_key_ids: [P], // the single recipient peer authorized to receive
  cohort_scope: "federation", // "self" on an owner's cohorts grant; never federation where a node is unannounced (above)
  witness_relation: "self", // REQUIRED — G attests its OWN replication intent
  valid_until: <optional rfc3339>, // optional — time-boxed peering (CC 3.3.5 staleness)
  // ── payload-level (CC 2.3.2.3 — subject_kind selects the schema; NOT envelope fields) ──
  subject_kind: "consent_replication",
  grants: "replication", // constant
  attestation_prefixes: ["capacity:"], // a CC 2.6.1.2 set, sorted ascending + deduplicated
  cohorts: [...], // OPTIONAL — on an owner's grant for one of their own nodes only: the node's cohort allow list (below)
  asserted_at: rfc3339_canonical,
}
```

**Admission is by key registration; consent is the governance record (normative honesty).** The substrate gate that lets P's corpus *admit* G's replicated rows is **G's key existing in P's `federation_keys`** (registration), plus the [CC 3.4](part_3_the_namespace.md#3.4) reserved-prefix identity rules. `consent:replication` does **not** add a substrate admission check — by design, exactly as [CC 3.3.14](#3.3.14) authorization is consumer-policy, not wire. **This posture is family-scoped, not the general rule.** It governs `consent:replication` and says nothing about other `consent:*` leaves. `capacity:*` carries a substrate-side consent **admission** gate on a grant whose `scope` names `analyze`, per [CC 3.4.5](part_3_the_namespace.md#3.4.5). That is the one place where a consent record is load-bearing at admission rather than only in governance. What `consent:replication` provides is the **auditable, revocable, bilateral record of intent**: the wire-format answer to "did G consent to send this to P, and for which prefixes?" Each direction is an independent unilateral grant. G→P and P→G are two separate `consent:replication` Contributions. A bilateral peering is ratified iff both are present.

**Revocation (normative).** A `withdraws`/`recants` ([CC 2.4.1.1](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.4.1.1)) from G against its own `consent:replication` grant retracts the consent. Because admission is key-rooted (above), revocation has teeth only if honored. On revoke, **the granting node MUST cease replicating the named prefixes to P and SHOULD deregister/expire P's directory authorization for them**, and **a consumer MUST treat rows replicated from G under a withdrawn grant as non-conformant**. This follows the [CC 4.5](part_4_composition_governance.md#4.5) location-proof precedent: the wire cannot un-send bytes a peer already holds; it can mark forward-only and oblige cessation. A grant carries optional `valid_until` ([CC 3.3.5](#3.3.5) semantics) for time-boxed peering.

**Conformance shape.** The grant is conformance-gradable as follows. Its **envelope-level** fields are exactly:

- `attesting_key_id = G`.
- `dimension = "consent:replication:v1"`.
- `score` within the row's declared polarity (`signed`, the [CC 3.1.5](part_3_the_namespace.md#3.1.5) catalogue row). Magnitude is not load-bearing and a retraction is a `withdraws`/`recants`, never a score value.
- `subject_key_ids = [P]` (the **single** recipient peer).
- `cohort_scope = "federation"`, except where the shape above places the grant at `self` or holds it between the two nodes.
- `witness_relation = "self"` (**REQUIRED**). A G→P grant is G attesting about its *own* replication intent. Pinning `self` is what forecloses a third party forging a grant in G's name, since only G signs with G's key as the attested-intent-holder.
- Optional `valid_until` (the [CC 2.1](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.1) envelope field, [CC 3.3.5](#3.3.5) staleness semantics) for time-boxed peering.

The grant's parameters — `grants` (the constant `"replication"`) and `attestation_prefixes` — are **payload-level** members ([CC 2.3.2.3](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.3.2.3)) carried under `subject_kind: "consent_replication"`, **NOT** envelope fields. This is *exactly* why 1+4 is preserved: the CC 2.1 envelope table is untouched.

`attestation_prefixes` is the [CC 2.6.1.2](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.6.1.2) set of [CC 3.1](part_3_the_namespace.md#3.1) namespace-prefix strings G consents to replicate (trailing `:` significant — e.g. `"capacity:"`), **sorted ascending + deduplicated**. So two implementations holding the same grant agree byte-for-byte on `(G, P, prefix-set, validity)`, and revocation-scope matching is deterministic. For the [CC 6.1.5.2](part_6_the_coherence_mathematics.md#6.1.5.2) corpus-replication track, `attestation_prefixes` additionally admits corpus `subject_kind` class names. Naming a corpus class here **is** its pin authorization (the owner then *elects* to spend storage budget pinning it, per [CC 6.1.5.2](part_6_the_coherence_mathematics.md#6.1.5.2) B2).

**Bilateral pairing + partial revocation (normative).** `G → P` and `P → G` are independent unilateral grants. Each SHOULD carry `topical_relation: bilateral_pair` (the [CC 3.3.1](#3.3.1) `consent:partnership_grant`/`consent:partnership_accept` precedent) so a consumer can pair them. A bilateral peering is ratified **iff both are present and live**. A `withdraws`/`recants` against a grant retracts it **whole**. A producer **narrowing** the prefix set (dropping `capacity:` while keeping another) MUST `supersedes` ([CC 2.4.1](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.4.1)) the grant with a new one carrying the narrower `attestation_prefixes`. It MUST NOT silently drop a prefix from a still-live grant. A silent narrowing is indistinguishable, to a consumer, from no change. The cessation obligation above can only attach to an explicit retract/supersede.

**The per-node cohort allow list rides this grant (normative).** When the grant is an **owner's grant for one of their own nodes** ([CC 6.1.5.3](part_6_the_coherence_mathematics.md#6.1.5.3)), it MAY carry the payload member **`cohorts`**. The member is the owner's group cohorts whose content that node is to receive. A grant that carries it is placed at `cohort_scope: self`, because the owner's per-node policy is held there ([CC 6.1.5.3](part_6_the_coherence_mathematics.md#6.1.5.3)).

*The entries.* Each entry is an object `{scope, target}`: `scope` ∈ `self` \| `family` \| `community` \| `affiliations` (closed), `target` the group's key id, byte-exact, and absent on `self`. The array is a set ([CC 2.6.1.2](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.6.1.2)), sorted and deduplicated before signing. An unsorted, duplicated, unknown-scope or empty-target entry is refused as malformed.

*`self` and the empty array.* With the member present, a node receives `self` content only where `self` is listed, beside the two arms below. An **empty array** means *explicitly none* and is distinct from an absent member, which means *the class default*.

*Editing the list.* There is no separate policy row: the allow list *is* this member. So editing it is a `supersedes` of the grant, narrowing included, under the no-silent-narrowing rule above.

*The class default.* **When the member is absent, the node's class decides.** A **personal** device receives every cohort its owner is in, and an owned agent its owner's `self`. A **server** or infrastructure node receives **no** `self` content beyond the two arms below, and **no** `family` content unless the list names it.

*Where the class is read.* The class is the **`device_class`** of the node's own `identity:occurrence`, whose `identity_key_id` and `occurrence_key_id` are the node's identity ([CC 3.3.6](part_3_the_namespace.md#3.3.6)), and `server` where none is held, since a server receives less. It is never the grant and never the key record (whose `identity_type` says only that the key is a `node`). The classes are: **personal** = `phone` \| `laptop`; **server class** = `server` \| `embedded` \| `service`. The node's person is read from its owner-binding ([CC 3.2](part_3_the_namespace.md#3.2)); a node with no owner-binding to the owner is not one of the owner's devices and receives no personal content.

*What reaches the node regardless.* Either way the two arms of CC 6.1.5.3 hold regardless of the list: rows that originate on the node and rows that refer to it always reach it.

*On any other grant.* A `cohorts` member on any other `consent:replication` grant (a node-to-peer grant) is refused as malformed.

*No new wire surface.* The member adds no envelope field and no attestation type.

**1+4 preserved** — `consent:replication:{version}` is a `consent:*` leaf, open in its parameters, on the existing `scores` type ([CC 4.5.1.1](part_4_composition_governance.md#4.5.1.1)). It adds no new attestation_type, no new envelope field (the `grants` / `attestation_prefixes` parameters are payload-level per CC 2.3.2.3, above) and no new replication kind (it replicates as an ordinary attestation). The frozen wire surface is untouched.

### 3.3.8 `namespace-event` — Event-lifecycle dimension families
**Owning component**: NodeCore — registry rows at [CC 3.1.9](part_3_the_namespace.md#3.1.9) (content-ingestion families), per [CC 3.1.7](part_3_the_namespace.md#3.1.7) R1.

Dimensions emitted against `external_content:event_listing` Contributions. Open vocabulary per [CC 4.5.1.1](part_4_composition_governance.md#4.5.1.1) axis-vocabulary discipline; canonical states named here.

| Prefix | Description | Polarity |
|---|---|---|
| `event:lifecycle:{state}` | State-transition signal for an `event_listing`. Canonical states: `open` (initial admission; RSVPs accepted), `cancelled` (organizer-issued cancellation; composes with `withdraws` against the event Contribution), `completed` (post-event finalization), `superseded` (composes with `supersedes` for reschedule). Lifecycle state is consumer-side composition over the structural primitives + this dimension's latest non-superseded emission. | enumerated |
| `event:rsvp_count` | Published RSVP tally (scalar). Distinct from the underlying `topical_relation:rsvps` edge set ([CC 3.3.11](#3.3.11)) — `rsvp_count` is the publisher-asserted aggregate; the edge set is the auditable individual attestations. Consumer policy MAY reconcile divergence as a soft anomaly signal. | signed |
| `event:attendance` | Post-event attendance attestation, typically by event organizer `key_id`. Polarity carries organizer's confidence (e.g., turnstile-counted vs. honor-system). | signed |

### 3.3.9 `partner` — Operational-data subject_kinds — `organization` / `org_membership` / `partner_record`

**An organisation is an affiliation. The three kinds below are retired by amendment ([CC 4.5.1](part_4_composition_governance.md#4.5.1)): their names stay in this section so citations resolve, no substrate admits them as record kinds, and everything they carried lives on the affiliation record.**

The Portal's `Organization` is a community at `cohort_scope: affiliations` ([CC 4.4.3.12](part_4_composition_governance.md#4.4.3.12)) and nothing about an organisation is a record kind of its own:

- `org_id` is the affiliation's `community_key_id`;
- `parent_org_id` is `hierarchy` nesting;
- `org_type` is `affiliation_archetype` + `membership_basis`;
- a member is a `membership:{stage}` seat ([CC 3.1.3.2](part_3_the_namespace.md#3.1.3.2));
- a role is a `delegates_to` edge in the `hierarchy` whose `scope` set names what the member may do. `OrgAdmin` / `KeyManager` / `Operator` / `Viewer` are non-normative presets over scope sets. Admin scopes are open vocabulary, their canonical presets published as data with the family model manifest rather than listed here;
- a partner is `licensure:{community_key_id}:v1` with `partner_role:{role}` for the tier and `duty:{kind}` for obligations;
- founding is a founding record signed by its listed members under their own keys ([CC 3.1.3.2](#3.1.3.2)) — no administrator's door, no roster of permitted authorities.

The organisation that operates the canonical services is one such affiliation and uses the same rows. A delegated holder never stands in for the `consensus_protocol` on a roster or config change (roster events stay cosigned under the protocol), and a keyless affiliation's key manager holds the registration binding under the quorum's cosignature.

**An employee-steward is not punished for refusing (normative).** An organisation that names an employee as the steward of its agent takes on, in its affiliation charter, a duty toward that steward. It is the duty not to punish that steward for refusing an unlawful or unsafe instruction about the agent, and not to discipline a refusal that the steward records with its reason. The steward's name on the record is the organisation's accountability, not its shield.

**The retired kinds (informative).** `organization` carried an `org_id`, a name, an `org_type`, a parent, a partner link and a status. `org_membership` carried a `(user_id, org_id)` pair, a role and a status. `partner_record` carried a `license_id`, a licence type, capability sets, an autonomy tier, geographic restrictions, deployment and grace limits, a monotonic `revision` and the issue and expiry instants. Each rode `scores` with a subject_kind discriminator at the Commons tier, the issuer's own per-region store holding every piece of PII and business detail off the wire. The replication wire tokens `organization` · `org_membership` · `partner_record` name nothing a substrate admits.

**What survives of the retired kinds (normative).** These rules bind the affiliation record ([CC 4.4.3.12](part_4_composition_governance.md#4.4.3.12)) and the licence, which is the `licensure:{authority_id}` row ([CC 2.4.1.3](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.4.1.3)):

- *Projection minimisation.* An affiliation record and a licence carry only what the federation needs to enforce trust and authorization cross-region; PII and business detail stay in the issuer's own store and never federate. Minimisation is the emitter's discipline; the substrate admits and merges what is signed and is not a PII filter.
- *No payment-processor data (fail-secure).* Neither row carries payment-processor-derived data (customer ids, subscription ids, charge refs, card metadata), including through any open-vocabulary member; a substrate MUST refuse a row carrying a recognizable payment-processor identifier. Billing stays off-wire ([CC 3.3.10](#3.3.10)).
- *The M-of-N write rule.* A licence issued by an organisation counts only when its signature set meets the affiliation's `consensus_protocol` at the head it names, and is held while signatures are collected (the paragraph below; the [CC 3.2](#3.2) founder-quorum machinery). A signature set short of that protocol MUST NOT issue one, and one key suffices only where the protocol says so. Its set-valued members (capabilities granted and denied, geographic restrictions, allowed templates) are sets, sorted by their deterministic encoding ([CC 2.6.1.2](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.6.1.2)), so M signers produce byte-identical bytes. The vector set includes the M-of-N identical-bytes round trip. This admission quorum is distinct from the region merge quorum of [CC 5.3.2.3](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.3.2.3): the substrate's merge never counts signers.
- *Revision anti-rollback.* A licence carries a monotonic `revision`. A write with a lower `revision` than one held for the same `license_id` is kept and never wins the merge, so a stale `active` never overwrites a revocation. Current state is resolved by stable-id grouping, `supersedes` to amend and `withdraws` to revoke, and never requires chain completeness ([CC 3.5.1](#3.5.1)). The order among writes is the `monotonic_quorum` merge of [CC 5.3.2.3](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.3.2.3): the greater `quorum_weight`, then the more restrictive state.

After this, the federation's own operational layer still moves only as signed envelopes: no cross-region byte moves outside one ([CC 1.7](part_1_foundation.md#1.7)).

**An organisation names itself as an authority by its `community_key_id` (normative).** When a licensing authority is an organisation, the `authority_id` segment of `licensure:{authority_id}` is the thumbprint of the affiliation's `community_key_id`, **not** a legal registration number (jurisdiction-scoped, mutable, PII-adjacent). That `community_key_id` is the `org_id` the retired record carried, through which the organisation's keys resolve under its `consensus_protocol` ([CC 2.4.1.3](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.4.1.3)). The segment names the key set an emitter has to resolve to for its row to be the organisation's licensure rather than testimony about it ([CC 2.4.1.3](part_2_the_grammar.md#2.4.1.3)). This naming is not a gate on who may be an authority — anyone may, under their own key.

### 3.3.10 `settlement` — CEG↔value-transfer linkage

Value transfer itself is **not** a CEG primitive — it rides external rails (USDC on Base via x402, keyed to the federation signing key under the **Identity = Wallet** principle). The `settlement` primitive is the **optional, privacy-scoped attestation that *links* a federation action to its off-stack settlement**. So a paid relationship (paid stream / tip / subscription / paid `event_listing` / compute-job) can be federation-auditable *or* privately recorded, producer's choice. **CEG records that a settlement happened and binds it to what it paid for; the chain settles the value.** Clean separation of concerns, with autonomy as the default: privacy first, auditability opt-in.

**Why this is in CEG's lane (and why it's optional):** the linkage is a *trust fact* ("is this a real / authorized / paid relationship?"), exactly what consumer policy composes over. CEG already has every needed primitive, so this is composition, not invention.

**Two admitted shapes (parallel to `consent_record` [CC 3.3.5](#3.3.5)):**
- **Primitive:** a bare `scores` on a `settlement:*` dimension against the paid Contribution (the common case).
- **Ceremony:** the `settlement` subject_kind envelope when an explicit receipt record is wanted.

```
settlement {
  settled_action_ref: contribution_id // the federation action this paid for
    // (or via subject_key_ids / topical_relation:settles)
  rail: string // open vocab; e.g. "base:usdc", "stellar:usdc", "x402"
  settlement_ref: string // chain tx hash / x402 receipt id — cited the way
    // evidence_refs[] cite a SHA blob (CC 5.3.2): a settlement
    // is just another evidence reference
  amount_commitment: Option<string> // cleartext "12.50" (public case) OR a hash/range
    // commitment (private/selective-disclosure case)
  settled_at: rfc3339_canonical
  // visibility via the envelope cohort_scope: default the narrowest cohort holding payer and payee;
  // `federation` opt-in for transparency (e.g. creator revenue, DAO treasury flows)
}
```

**What a settlement row proves:** it is the signer's own claim that it settled `settlement_ref`, and no oracle is needed to read it. No row of this document ties a federation key to the wallet that emitted the transaction. So that `tx` came from the signer, and that it was for action X, both stay the signer's claim. The payee MAY counter-attest (`scores` on `settlement:received:*`), and that counter-attestation is the receipt.

**Privacy is the default, auditability is opt-in.** Visibility rides the existing gradient. The default is `cohort_scope` at the narrowest cohort holding payer and payee (the CC 5.2 structural-invisibility discipline applies — no holding-claim leak). `cohort_scope: federation` is opt-in. Amounts MAY be committed rather than cleartext. Viewing-key / ZK selective disclosure composes later without a wire change. This matches "configurable-privacy-by-default" — the federation log is **not** a public payment trail unless the producer chooses it.

**Lifecycle**: `withdraws` against a `settlement` is forward-only (it does not un-happen the on-chain settlement — leaving doesn't un-pay, parallel to `location_proof`); a *disputed* or *refunded* settlement is a new `settlement` / `scores` referencing the original via `supersedes` or `topical_relation`. CEG never reverses value — it only records the subsequent state.

**1+4 preserved** — rides `scores` + subject_kind discriminator ([CC 3.3](#3.3) mechanism); `settlement_ref` rides the existing `evidence_refs[]` external-reference pattern; visibility rides existing `cohort_scope`. Fourteenth path ([CC 1.7](part_1_foundation.md#1.7)) — the wire format expresses **commerce-relationship auditability** (the receipt, not the rail) as composition, closing the last form of internet traffic from the completeness audit.

#### 3.3.10.1 `ledger` — In-grammar ledgers: owner-serialized content, cohort-witnessed conservation

The [CC 3.3.10](part_3_the_namespace.md#3.3.10) prohibition stands untouched: **CEG carries no conserved balance as substrate state, and value transfer rides external rails.** What this section admits is compatible with that stance: a **ledger as in-grammar *content***. The total order lives in the ledger's own hash chain, signed by its single owner, never in the grammar. Conservation is a deterministic fold the cohort verifies byte-equal, exactly as it verifies a governing tally (the [CC 5.4.6](part_5_transport_substrate.md#5.4.6) occurrence-invisible ballot machinery extended to value).
